name: Carlos Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to any of it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the payment support team for an energy supplier, in an old textile mill in the middle of town that they turned into a contact centre. Most of my calls are people who can't pay their gas and electric bill, so I set up payment plans and check if they qualify for hardship help. I start at nine, finish at half five, and do maybe forty calls a day. The good part is when someone's crying at the start and calm at the end because we've found a plan that works.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been doing it, and how's it going?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: About a year and a half. I'm not the quickest, and I still have to look up the hardship rules every time because they keep changing. Sometimes I use the chat assistant the company gave us to tidy up the follow-up emails, but only when I'm behind. I share a flat with my cousin Daniel, who works at the tyre place, and after rent and bills I've got a couple of weeks of money spare at best.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first of five pictures of the future. This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. That's roughly what my supervisor thinks will happen, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, because the people who ring us need a human, not a menu. I'd probably post something like that, about how energy debt isn't a problem you fix with a chatbot. At work we'd joke that the email assistant was the peak of the revolution.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my job's probably safe in that one. Energy firms get fined if they treat struggling customers badly, so they keep people like me on the hardship line. The worry is just the usual one, my pay is low and the rent went up again in September.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, and actually use the email tool properly so I'm not always behind. I'd put my name down for the vulnerable customers training they run every spring, because that comes with a small pay bump. And I'd try to put fifty a month away, which I've never managed before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. A bit flat, because it means nothing changes, including my pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the rent went up. How tight is it now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight enough that I check my balance before I buy a coffee. Daniel and I split everything down the middle, and if one of us is short the other covers it, but we're both on low wages. One broken boiler and we'd be in trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the pay bump from the training mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About a hundred a month before tax. That's the difference between saving nothing and saving something. My supervisor says I'd be good at it because I'm patient, even if I'm slow.

say: I'd say people with **energy debt** need a human, not a chatbot menu.
At work I'd joke that the **email assistant** was the peak of the revolution.
think: His job looks **safe** because regulators fine energy firms that mistreat struggling customers.
The real worry is **low pay** and a rent rise in September.
do: Use the **email tool** properly so he's no longer behind on follow-ups.
Sign up for the spring **vulnerable customers** training and its pay bump.
Try to save **fifty a month** for the first time.
feel: **Mostly fine**, but a bit **flat**, because his pay doesn't change either.
S0.quote: Energy debt isn't a problem you fix with a chatbot.
fieldNote: He trusts **regulation** to protect his role, which fits his progressive views.
His pressure is **money**, not job loss, in this picture.
He's open to the email tool once it's **proven useful**, not before.

steps.text: Keep handling payment plans on the hardship line
Use the company email assistant for every follow-up email
Join the spring vulnerable customers training for the pay bump
Set up a fifty-a-month standing order into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Answering customers. Yeah, that's us. That's the first thing they'd try.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say they can automate the meter readings and the address changes, fine, but keep humans on the hardship line. I'd say that at work and I'd sign anything the union put out about it. I'd also say the savings should go into lower bills, not bonuses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think the simple calls go to the bot first, and then the team shrinks because there are fewer calls left. The hardship line is the hard stuff, so it'd last longer, but they'd want fewer of us and faster. I'm slow, so I could be one of the ones who goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get properly good at whatever tool they bring in, once I see it actually works, because the people who use it well will be the ones they keep. I'd join the union, which I've been meaning to do for a year. And I'd look at the free debt adviser course the money charity runs, because that's the same work outside a call centre.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy in my stomach. Like I'm on probation again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn the tool once it works. How would you know?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When the people on my bank of desks start hitting their targets with it and not getting complaints. I'm not going to be the first, but I won't be the last either. I'd ask Priya, who's always first with these things, to show me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first if your hours were reduced?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The phone contract, I'd go to a cheap SIM-only deal. Then the gym, then eating out with Daniel on Fridays. Food and rent are the only things I can't touch.

say: I'd say automate the **simple calls** but keep humans on the **hardship line**.
I'd argue the savings should go into **lower bills**, not bonuses.
think: The **team shrinks** as simple calls go to the bot.
Because he's **slow**, he could be one of the people let go.
do: Learn the new tool well **once colleagues show** it works.
Finally **join the union**, after a year of meaning to.
Look at the free **debt adviser course** run by the money charity.
feel: **Uneasy** in his stomach, like being **on probation** again.
S1.quote: I'm not going to be the first, but I won't be the last either.
fieldNote: He waits for **proof** before adopting a tool, then commits.
He sees the **debt adviser** route as the same work outside the call centre.
His cut list stops at **food and rent**, showing how little slack he has.

steps.text: Learn the new call tool from the colleague who adopts first
Join the union at the energy contact centre
Enrol on the money charity's free debt adviser course
Switch to a cheap SIM-only phone deal

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? That's not even enough time to finish a course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this has to be handled by the government, not left to the energy companies. People like the ones I talk to every day would be losing their jobs and then not paying their bills. I'd be posting about a basic income, and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my job is gone. Even the hardship line is thinking work, it's rules and listening, and an AI that can do any thinking job can do that. Robots come three years later, so the only safe-ish work for a while is with your hands, and I've never done that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd ask Daniel's boss at the tyre place if they need anyone, even just sweeping and fitting. I'd stop saving for anything long term and keep every penny as a buffer. I'd sign up with the union's hardship fund and make sure I know what benefits I'd get.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, honestly. I'd be the one on the other end of the hardship line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd go from setting up payment plans to needing one. What would that be like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Humiliating, a bit, but I know the system better than most. I'd know exactly what to ask for and which forms to fill in. That's the strange thing, my job would be useful to me right at the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the tyre place really work as a plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For three years, maybe. Fitting tyres is hands-on, so it's safe until the robots come around 2031. After that I don't know, and I'd be thirty, with no savings and two trades that are both gone.

say: I'd say the **government** must handle this, not the energy companies.
I'd post in favour of a **basic income**, and mean it.
think: Even the hardship line is **thinking work**, so his job goes.
Hands-on work is safe for only about **three years**, and he has none.
do: Ask Daniel's boss at the **tyre place** for any hands-on work.
Keep every penny as a **buffer** instead of saving long term.
Sign up for the **union hardship fund** and check benefits.
feel: **Scared**, picturing himself as the caller on the **hardship line**.
S2.quote: My job would be useful to me right at the end.
fieldNote: The irony of needing his own **payment plan** hits him hard.
He reads the **three-year robot gap** clearly and plans around it.
His only hands-on lead is through his **cousin**.

steps.text: Ask the tyre place manager for fitting or yard work
Hold all spare money as a cash buffer
Register with the union hardship fund and check benefits
Post and campaign online for a basic income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a bit more breathing room, but not much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I said before, that the money from this has to be shared out. But I'd add that five years is enough time to plan, so there's no excuse. I'd be at the union meetings asking what the plan is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I've got maybe three of those years in the call centre. Then the job's gone, and I'd want to be in something with my hands by then. The robots would come about 2034, so that buys a bit more time again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the evening electrical course at the college in the first year, because that's hands-on and there's always work. I'd use the AI tools at work as much as I could, to keep my numbers up while I study. I'd try to save a hundred a month, so I have something when the call centre goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but like I've got something to grab. Not falling, but on a ledge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why electrical work and not the debt advice you mentioned earlier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because debt advice is thinking work, and that's the first thing to go in this one. Electrical is hands-on, and it gives me until the robots arrive. I'd rather be wiring houses than out of work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you pay for the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The college does a low-income discount, so it's about two hundred a term. I'd skip a holiday and the Friday takeaways. My mum might help a bit too, she offered when I started the call centre job.

say: I'd say the **money** from AI has to be shared out.
I'd ask the **union** what the plan is, since five years leaves no excuse.
think: He expects about **three years** left in the call centre.
Hands-on work buys more time, until robots around **2034**.
do: Start the evening **electrical course** at the college in year one.
Use the **AI tools** at work to keep his numbers up.
Save **a hundred** a month for when the job goes.
feel: **Worried**, but with something to grab, like being **on a ledge**.
S3.quote: I'd rather be wiring houses than out of work.
fieldNote: He switches from **debt advice** to electrical work because he sees thinking work goes first.
He uses **AI** as a bridge to keep his job while training.
His mother is a **quiet backstop** he only mentions when pressed.

steps.text: Enrol on the evening electrical course at the local college
Use the call centre AI tools on every shift
Put a hundred a month into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That feels a lot more doable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this right, so we should demand it be done right. Free training, proper notice, and a share of the savings going back to workers. That's what I'd be saying at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's okay for me if I don't waste it. The call centre job probably goes before 2036, but I'd have time for a proper apprenticeship and even a few years working in it. It's my habit of waiting until everyone else moves that worries me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going on the phones for now and get good at the tools. In a year or two I'd start an electrical apprenticeship or the debt adviser course, depending on what's working for others. I'd join the union now, because that's the easiest thing to do today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer. Still worried about money, but there's a road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd wait a year or two to start. What would you be watching for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether the people who left early are doing well. If Priya's doing debt advice and loving it, I'd follow. If the electricians are all busy, I'd go that way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the one thing that would make this go wrong for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent going up faster than my pay. If I can't save anything, I can't afford to train, and then ten years goes by and I'm just older. That's the honest risk.

say: I'd say ten years is enough to **do it right**, so we should demand it.
I'd push for **free training**, notice and a share of the savings.
think: The phone job likely goes **before 2036**, but there's time to retrain.
His **habit of waiting** for others is the real risk.
do: Stay on the phones and get good at the **AI tools**.
Start an **apprenticeship** or debt course in a year or two.
Join the **union** now, the easiest step today.
feel: **Calmer**, still worried about money, but with **a road** ahead.
S4.quote: If I can't save anything, I can't afford to train, and then ten years goes by and I'm just older.
fieldNote: Ten years turns his **steady** style from a risk into a reasonable plan.
He names **rent rises** as the thing that could stop him training.
He still copies **early movers** rather than leading.

steps.text: Keep working the hardship line for the next year
Practise with the AI tools on every call
Join the union at the energy contact centre this month
Start an electrical apprenticeship or debt course within two years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there's no time to learn anything. What would help is a training wage, so I could learn a trade without losing the flat. And keeping energy bills down for people like me, because otherwise I'd be calling my own team.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how many of us are one bill away from trouble already. I talk to people one bill away from trouble all day, and I'm not far off being one of them.

headlineQuote: I talk to people one bill away from trouble all day, and I'm not far off being one of them.
portrait: Carlos is a **27-year-old** agent on an energy supplier's **hardship line**, setting up payment plans for struggling customers.
He shares a flat with his cousin, earns **low pay**, and has a couple of weeks of savings.
He leans left and wants **regulation**, unions and shared gains to protect workers.
He adopts tools **once proven** by colleagues, and his plans shift from debt advice to electrical work.
He's uneasy in the calm pictures and **alarmed** when AGI arrives within five years.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture worries him most, because there's **no time** to learn anything.
whatWouldHelp: A **training wage** so he can learn a trade without losing his flat.
Lower **energy bills** for low earners like himself.
